newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco deal euphoria tempered by review process.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco deal euphoria tempered by review process.

text.p: Initial euphoria over the landmark agreement between U.S. states and the tobacco industry was tempered on Saturday by the prospect of months of painstaking review by the White House, Congress and public health groups.

Tobacco companies on Friday agreed to pay a massive $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and accept extensive federal regulation over their products and advertising in return for immunity from further punitive liability for any past deception, fraud or conspiracy.

As state attorneys general -- who negotiated the deal with company executives over almost three months -- celebrated their success, cautionary flags were raised by President Bill Clinton, lawmakers, medical groups and health activists.
Clinton reserved judgment on the agreement, saying the administration would study it for several weeks to see if it met U.S. public health interests.

He directed chief domestic policy adviser Bruce Reed and Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala to consult public health officials and others and to subject the pact "to the strictest scrutiny."
"We must now carefully consider whether approving this proposed settlement will protect the public health -- and particularly our children's health -- to the greatest extent possible," Clinton said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters he expected the evaluation of the deal to take "a matter of weeks." Other U.S. officials said the two aides had been given four to six weeks to conduct the review.
The costly and politically sensitive settlement will require complex legislation from Congress to put it into effect and several senior members signalled that would not be forthcoming anytime soon.

"We'll be glad to look at what they think their settlement is ... whether or not that becomes law will be a function of the congressional committees, the hearing process," said House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican.
Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin of Iowa warned "the devil is in the details" and said the deal needed to emerge from "smoke-filled rooms into the sunshine of the public arena."

The likely scenario is a tug-of-war, with tobacco foes trying to toughen up the deal, and lawmakers from tobacco-producing states trying to ensure the industry does not lose more than already agreed at the bargaining table.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott indicated it could be months before Congress considered any agreement. The Mississippi Republican said the Congressional agenda was so packed he thought it unlikely to come up until autumn.

Health groups also want to take a long, close look at the deal. While the American Cancer Society and the American Medical Association have been supportive of a settlement, they reacted warily, refusing to take a final position pending extensive reviews of the terms.

Other prominent organizations, among them the American Lung Association and smaller anti-smoking actvist groups, were more skeptical, fearing the tobacco industry would be able to reshape any settlement to its own advantage in Congress.

Nevertheless, the agreement marked a severe defeat for the proud and powerful U.S. tobacco industry that has boasted for decades it would never settle a smoking case and has denied that cigarettes are addictive or cause lung cancer.

Facing the prospect of massive and unprecedented litigation, the industry said it was swallowing a "bitter pill" by accepting legislative and regulatory provisions with which it did not necessarily agree.

"But on balance, this plan is preferable to a continuation of a decades-long controversy that has failed to produce a constructive outcome for anyone," said Philip Morris Senior Vice President Steven Parrish.
